title: Netflix Conductor: The Next Chapter
summary:
Netflix Conductor : The Next Chapter

by Aravindan Ramkumar on behalf of the Conductor team

Conductor is the workflow orchestration engine Netflix uses to stitch micro-services into reliable, observable business processes.

If you’ve followed Conductor from the outside, the last thing you heard was probably the note on its GitHub repository: Netflix discontinued maintenance of Conductor OSS to refocus its resources on the internal fork.

That announcement marked the end of the open-source chapter, and from the outside it may have looked like the end of the story. It wasn’t. Internally, Conductor never slowed down. If anything, it grew faster, and the demands of that growth pushed us to rebuild it from the ground up. This post is the answer to the natural question that announcement leaves open: what happened to Conductor after that?

A lot, it turns out. The clearest way to put it is in terms of growth. Not long ago, Conductor crossing a billion workflow executions in a single year felt like a milestone. Today it clears that bar roughly every quarter, and the monthly volume is still climbing. Sustaining that kind of growth meant rethinking nearly every layer of the system. The data plane it runs on was modernized piece by piece. The evaluation engine was rewritten. The way it allocates work, controls concurrency, and runs compute all changes. The through-line is simple: scale forced a rethink of the evaluation engine and the layers beneath it, and everything else followed.

The rest of this post walks through that evolution: how the architecture changed, the performance and scale work at the heart of it, the leap forward in developer experience, and the newer capabilities for controlling how workflows and tasks execute.

How Netflix uses Conductor

When we last wrote about Conductor, it ran a few hundred workflow definitions for a few dozen teams. That footprint has grown by orders of magnitude. Conductor now backs roughly 200,000 workflow definitions owned by around 150 applications, spanning Content and Studio Engineering, Ads, Games, and more. The runtime side has grown to match. In a typical month it executes on the order of 420 million workflows, and on a given day it runs anywhere from 5 to 20 million, with teams adding hundreds of new workflow types every month.

Conductor and the Media Production Suite

One of the clearest ways to see what Conductor does is Netflix’s Media Production Suite (MPS). It’s a set of applications that move production data into the cloud. An average Netflix title generates around 200 terabytes of original camera files, and MPS is what gets that media ingested, validated, transcoded, and delivered to the right people around the world.

The multi-step pipelines behind MPS’s workflows (Footage Ingest, Dailies, VFX Pulls, and Conform Pulls) run as Conductor workflows. A dedicated orchestration layer called Studio Orchestrator stitches together the platform services these pipelines depend on, such as asset management, media encoding, and storage, using Conductor under the hood to ensure reliable execution and the durability to recover from the inevitable failures of long-running, distributed work.

Beyond the studio: Ads and Games

Content engineering is where Conductor started, but it’s no longer the whole story. Two of Netflix’s newer businesses lean on it just as heavily.

Netflix Ads has made Conductor a backbone of its programmatic pipelines. Creative ingestion, advertiser-certificate management, and privacy-preserving Data Clean Rooms all run as Conductor workflows.

Netflix Games uses Conductor to orchestrate the path a game takes from a partner’s submission to the app stores. When a studio uploads a build, a Conductor pipeline ingests the binary, runs the required validations (for example, iOS privacy-manifest checks), and drives App Store publishing, coordinating steps that span multiple platform services and external stores with the same reliability and visibility the studio pipelines rely on.

How the architecture evolved

Our earlier post described a Conductor built on a particular set of building blocks: DynoQueues for queueing, Dynomite for metadata, Cassandra (partially) for execution data, and Elasticsearch for indexing. That stack carried Conductor a long way, but as adoption climbed, almost every layer of it was eventually rethought. The data plane Conductor runs on today looks very little like the earlier one.

1.0: the original stack, and where it strained

In its first generation, Conductor leaned heavily on Dynomite (with DynoQueues as the queueing recipe layered on top) backed by Elasticsearch for indexing. It worked, but two classes of problems showed up as scale grew. The first was the datastore. Dynomite is an in-memory store: a clustering layer that adds sharding and replication on top of Redis. You scale it by adding memory and nodes, with each replica rack holding a full copy of the data, which suits a cache but not the durable record for millions of workflows a day. Dyno Queues, built on the same store, inherited those limits, and its zone-sharded design made task scheduling uneven. The second was the engine’s design: evaluation ran synchronously and mutated workflow state in several places, so competing updates could leave a workflow inconsistent with no automated way to repair it.

The 2.x line was a sustained campaign to address these, and two replacements did most of the heavy lifting.

2.0: Cassandra as the backbone

The most consequential change was making Cassandra the primary datastore for execution data, displacing Dynomite. Cassandra gave Conductor the elastic, horizontal scaling it needed, and removed the scaling ceiling and zone-affinity constraints that the old datastore imposed. Around the same time, large task inputs and outputs were offloaded to S3, keeping bulky data off the primary datastore and further easing the pressure on it.

Timestone: a purpose-built queueing layer

The second replacement was the queue itself. Timestone, Netflix’s high-throughput, low-latency priority queueing system, took over from DynoQueues. Beyond shedding the Dynomite dependency, it brought two capabilities that mattered for reliability: a delayed-queuing mechanism, and a background repair process that could detect and recover workflows. Timestone also turned out to be foundational for work that came later. The async evaluation queue and the queue-depth-driven dynamic thread allocation described later in this post both build on it.

Alongside these, the 2.x series also decoupled indexing from the critical path, moving to a Kafka-buffered, independently scalable indexer writing to Elasticsearch.

3.0: consolidating the modern data plane

By Conductor 3.0, these threads came together into a coherent platform. Dynomite was fully sunset. Timestone was the queue and Cassandra the datastore. A Kafka-fed indexer pushed to Elasticsearch, with Iceberg added for long-term storage. The release also shipped automated workflow repair and multi-cluster deployment, the last of which lets workflows run in fully isolated contexts (for example, a dedicated context for the Media Production Suite, kept separate from the shared default and scaled on its own).

The net effect is that by 3.0 the foundational reliability and scaling problems of the early era were largely solved, and the data plane reached roughly the shape it has today.

Rebuilding the engine: Conductor 4.0

By 3.0, everything around the evaluation engine had been modernized, but the engine and its data model were largely the original, and at this scale that became the bottleneck. The engine evaluated a workflow by loading its entire state into memory to decide what to do next, which meant heavy memory pressure and slow evaluations as workflows grew toward tens of thousands of tasks. It also stored a workflow’s metadata and its task payloads in the same Cassandra partition, producing oversized “wide rows” and leaving room for race conditions when several updates to the same task competed. Evaluation overhead, vertical-scaling pressure, and occasional inconsistent state needed to be addressed.

A partitioned task model

The old data model co-located everything about a workflow in one place. The rewrite separates workflow metadata from task and user data and gives each task its own record. The engine no longer loads the whole workflow graph to make a decision. It evaluates against a lightweight blueprint of the workflow and loads only the specific task data a decision needs. The practical result is a dramatically smaller memory footprint per evaluation and far less work to advance a workflow by one step.

The 3.0 engine topped out around 2,500 tasks per workflow. The rewritten engine scales to 30,000 tasks per workflow, more than a 10x increase. Evaluation got faster too: in production, the rewrite delivered roughly a 40% reduction in p99 workflow-evaluation latency.

Making competing updates safe using partitions

Separating the data is only half the story. The engine also has to make competing updates to the same task safe, because a task can be written from more than one place at once. Picture a long-running task whose worker sends periodic updates to keep it alive, each one marking the task in-progress, before finally reporting it COMPLETED. If a stray in-progress update arrives just after that completion, reordered by the network, it could quietly revert a COMPLETED task back to IN_PROGRESS.

The first version leaned on Cassandra lightweight transactions (LWT) to serialize these writes, but mixing LWT with ordinary writes is a known Cassandra anti-pattern. The two use different timestamping mechanisms, and combining them breaks the strict consistency Conductor needs.

So the data model evolved away from locking entirely. Task state is split across two partitions: a pending partition for tasks still in flight, and a terminal partition that a task is written to exactly once, when it reaches a terminal state (COMPLETED, FAILED, etc). When the engine evaluates a workflow, it reads both and reconciles them in the application layer with one simple rule: a terminal state always wins over a non-terminal one, and between two writes of the same kind (two in-progress, or two terminal) ordinary last-write-wins applies. So in the race above, when the task is marked COMPLETED it lands in the terminal partition, and the late in-progress update loses on read.

The net of the rewrite is reliable task lifecycle management, a lower memory footprint, faster evaluation, and far higher concurrent throughput.

Removing the last synchronous bottleneck: async workflow evaluation

A faster engine still left one structural problem. Workflow evaluation ran synchronously. When an update arrived, a new workflow or a task completing, the request itself evaluated the workflow, and to do that safely it had to take a lock on that workflow. Under load, concurrent updates to the same workflow raced for that lock. Only one won, and the rest were deferred to a background repair process that, in extreme cases, could take several minutes to catch up. The result was exactly the kind of unpredictable tail latency that hurts most under peak load.

The fix was to decouple the trigger from the evaluation. Updates no longer evaluate inline. Instead they enqueue the workflow onto a Timestone exclusive queue, and a central asynchronous evaluator processes each workflow’s pending work in order. Because the queue is exclusive, only one worker ever evaluates a given workflow at a time, so the lock contention simply goes away.

The results are most dramatic at the tail (p99 and p99.9), which is the point, since the tail is what users feel under load:

Unsuccessful lock-acquire attempts, which had spiked to around 2,700 per interval under contention, drop to essentially zero with async evaluation.

Controlling how workflows execute

Run Strategies: native control over workflow concurrency

For most of its life, Conductor would happily run as many instances of a workflow as you started, all at once. That’s the right default, but it left a gap. When several workflow instances act on the same entity, the same movie id, the same creative, the same script, there is no built-in way to serialize them or guarantee only one runs at a time. Teams that needed this had to build it themselves: custom locks, custom queues, custom coordination logic bolted onto their workflows. That’s extra complexity in every workflow that needs it, and a real source of operational risk.

Run Strategies are a way to declare, on a workflow definition, how concurrent executions should be handled. There are two strategies today. Parallel, the default, applies no restrictions and behaves exactly as workflows always have. Sequential runs at most one workflow at a time per sequence key, with subsequent requests enqueued and started automatically, in order, as each running workflow finishes. A run strategy is declared on the workflow definition, and can be set directly in the Workflow SDK as a @RunStrategy annotation argument on the @WorkflowMethod.

The key idea is the sequence key: two executions that share a sequence key run one after another, and executions with different keys still run in parallel. So a content-ingestion workflow keyed on movie id processes each title strictly serially while happily running many different titles concurrently, with no custom locking required.

Beyond polled workers: managed, serverless tasks

A task meant a polled worker: your application implements the worker, polls the Conductor server for work, runs it, and reports the result back. That model is simple and language-agnostic, and it’s still the backbone for most workloads. But it has a cost. You operate the worker fleet. You stand it up, keep it running, and scale it, even for work that’s bursty or runs rarely.

So Conductor added managed tasks: built-in task types where Conductor drives the compute directly, with no long-lived worker for you to host or scale. Two integrations carry most of this today: Titus for containers and Stratum for serverless media-processing functions.

A TITUS task launches a Titus job to run a script, whether shell, Python, or whatever your image packages, using Titus, Netflix’s container management platform, as the compute plane. You point the task at a Docker image and an entry point, and specify the shape of the run, such as cpu and memory. The lifecycle is fully managed. The task starts IN_PROGRESS, Conductor monitors the Titus job, and it transitions on the container’s exit behavior. An exit code of 0 marks the task COMPLETED, and a non-zero code, a timeout, or a missing job marks it FAILED. The upshot is that you can spin up containerized compute as a step in a workflow without running a worker that sits around polling.

A STRATUM task invokes a Stratum function and collects its output. Stratum is the serverless function layer of Netflix’s Cosmos platform, purpose-built for media-processing workloads, and a Conductor STRATUM task is the natural way to call one from a workflow. You give it a function name and an ordered list of arguments. The task stays IN_PROGRESS until the function finishes, then resolves to COMPLETED, FAILED, or TIMED_OUT. Because Stratum exposes functions to Conductor directly, teams can fold resource-intensive media operations into a workflow without owning the compute that runs them.

Polled workers, Titus jobs, and Stratum functions are three points on a spectrum, and a single workflow can mix all three: a long-lived worker for steady high-volume work, a Titus container for an occasional heavy batch step, and a Stratum function for media processing. Managed tasks shift the operational burden from the team to the platform.

Scaling task polling: dynamic thread allocation

The engine work in the previous section made Conductor evaluate workflows fast. But there’s a second half to throughput: how quickly workers pick up the tasks that evaluation schedules. That’s a polling problem, and at scale it has its own failure mode, one that showed up most sharply for Studio Orchestrator, the heavy Conductor user behind the Media Production Suite pipelines from earlier in this post.

Conductor clients poll for work using worker threads, and historically the number of threads was fixed per task type. That’s predictable, and it prevents any one task from starving the others, but it’s static. During burst traffic, when thousands of instances of a single task suddenly pile into a queue, a fixed thread count can’t ramp up to drain them. The symptom was distinctive: CPU on the instances stayed flat while queues backed up, and idle threads sat stranded on quiet queues unable to help the overloaded one.

Allocating threads by real-time queue depth

The fix is a dynamic allocation strategy that rebalances threads across task queues continuously, based on how much work each queue actually has, while still guaranteeing every queue a floor so nothing starves.

Each instance periodically polls Timestone for the current depth of every task queue it manages. It then splits its thread pool into two parts. A minimum allocation gives every queue a baseline number of threads, so no queue is ever fully starved. A floating pool holds the remaining threads, distributed across queues in proportion to each queue’s share of the total load. A queue with a deep backlog draws a large slice of the floating pool. An idle queue falls back toward its minimum, freeing threads for whoever needs them.

One guardrail keeps this from becoming its own problem: a multiplier ceiling. A queue’s thread count can grow by at most a configurable factor per cycle, so even a dramatic load spike ramps up in controlled steps rather than all at once, giving downstream and dependent services time to absorb the increase instead of being bombarded. Allocations are recomputed every polling interval, so the system tracks shifting load in near real time while always honoring the per-queue minimums.

Two things come out of this. First, because threads are allocated where they’re actually needed, each instance can safely run a much larger pool. Second, CPU utilization becomes an accurate signal of how busy an instance is, which means autoscaling on CPU makes the cluster scale out in response to real computational demand.

Developer experience: Workflow SDK

For most of Conductor’s life, authoring a workflow meant writing JSON. You declared each task, then wired one task’s output into the next with ${taskRef.output.field} string templates, and on the worker side you pulled inputs back out of a Map<String, Object> and cast them to the types you expected. It worked, but it pushed an entire class of errors to runtime, and made large workflows genuinely hard to read.

The Workflow SDK is our answer: a type-safe Java DSL for authoring Conductor workflows. You write Java code. The compiler and IDE catch mistakes before anything deploys, and a Gradle plugin translates your Java code into the JSON workflow definition the Conductor server understands.

Crucially, the SDK gives you the best of both worlds. One of Conductor’s defining strengths has always been visibility. Because a workflow is a declared graph rather than imperative code, during execution the exact control flow can be inspected, every branch, loop, and parallel fork, and light up live as an execution moves through it. Writing workflows in imperative code gives you none of that. A timeline is not a workflow diagram. The SDK keeps both halves. You write in idiomatic Java and at execution time you still get the full visual graph: the same task-by-task flow, inputs and outputs, and at-a-glance “where is this stuck and why” that Conductor has always offered.

The authoring pains it removes

No type safety. In the JSON model, a task input like “movieId”: “${awesomeTask2.output.movieId}” is just a string template. The worker reads it back with inputData.get(“movieId”) and casts. If the upstream value is actually an Integer and you cast to String, you get a ClassCastException at runtime. Fix that, and a subtle typo bites next: the JSON declares an input variable movieId but the worker reads inputData.get(movieid), which returns null and you get a NullPointerException downstream. None of this is visible until the workflow runs.

public class GetMovieWorker implements Worker {
  @Override
  public TaskResult execute(Task task) {
    Map<String, Object> inputData = task.getInputData();
    long movieId = (Integer) inputData.get("movieId"); // cast, fingers crossed
    // more logic here
  }
}

Verbosity. Defining a couple of tasks is already wordy. A real workflow’s JSON balloons into hundreds of lines that are difficult to review or refactor. A complex branching workflow becomes a single large JSON blob that no one wants to touch.

{
 "name": "wrap_movie_workflow",
 "version": 1,
 "semver": "0.0.1", 
 "schemaVersion": 2,
 "restartable": true,
 "workflowStatusListenerEnabled": false,
 "ownerEmail": "team@netflix.com",
 "timeoutPolicy": "ALERT_ONLY",
 "timeoutSeconds": 0,
 "tasks": [
   {
     "name": "get_movie",
     "taskReferenceName": "movie",
     "type": "SIMPLE",
     "inputParameters": {
       "movieId": "${workflow.input.movieId}"
     }     
   },
   {     
     "name": "wrap_movie",
     "taskReferenceName": "wrapMovie",
     "type": "SIMPLE",
     "inputParameters": {
       "movie": "${movie.output}"
     }
   }
 ]
}

How the Java DSL works

@TaskMethod
public Movie getMovie(long movieId) { /* real worker logic */ }

@TaskMethod
public WrappedMovie wrapMovie(Movie movie) { /* real worker logic */ }
@WorkflowStub(taskNames = {"movieapp.getMovie", "movieapp.wrapMovie"})
public interface MovieWorkflows {
  @WorkflowGenerated(name = "movieapp.getMovie")
  Movie getMovie(int movieId);

  @WorkflowGenerated(name = "movieapp.wrapMovie")
  WrappedMovie wrapMovie(Movie movie);

  @WorkflowMethod(name = "wrap_movie_workflow", ownerEmail = "team@netflix.com")
  default WrappedMovie wrapMovieWorkflow(MovieInput input) {
    Movie movie = getMovie(input.getMovieId());  // long in, Movie out (checked)
    return wrapMovie(movie);                     // Movie in, WrappedMovie out (checked)
  }
}

The DSL has two core building blocks. The first, @TaskMethod, is a method that is executed at runtime and can contain arbitrary code. Crucially, it takes and returns real types: a getMovie task can take a long movieId and return a Movie object directly, with no maps and no casts. The second, @WorkflowMethod, is a method that is not executed and cannot contain arbitrary code. It expresses the workflow as ordinary method calls (call getMovie(…), then pass the result to wrapMovie(…)), and a Gradle build plugin parses it into a Conductor JSON definition at build time. The server does not see the Java code. It gets the same JSON it always has.

Code generation is central to how this works. In the @WorkflowStub annotation you declare the task and workflow names you want to use, and at build time the Gradle plugin generates their input and output types along with typed stub methods that you call inside a @WorkflowMethod. Those generated stubs are what let the method body compile against real signatures with full type safety. Because the stubs are generated from names rather than shared code, teams can reuse each other’s tasks and workflows without sharing libraries.

Real control flow, expressed in Java

The examples above are linear, but most production workflows branch, loop, and fan out. The DSL expresses these as the Java constructs you’d reach for anyway, and the SDK parses them into the corresponding Conductor operators. A useful mental model: you’re describing a workflow graph in Java, not running Java, so the parser only supports the constructs that map cleanly to Conductor (if/else, switch, do-while, parallel forks, sub-workflow calls) and asks you to express a few things its way. Iteration, for instance, is always a do-while, since there are no for or while tasks in Conductor.

A common shape is to kick off work, poll until it settles, then branch on the outcome, which is a do-while loop wrapped around an if/else:

@WorkflowMethod(name = "process_asset_workflow", ownerEmail = "team@netflix.com")
default void processAssetWorkflow(AssetInput input) {
  JobStatus status = submitJob(input);

  do {                                        // loops are do-while
    status = checkStatus(input.getJobId());
  } while (status.getState() == "PENDING");

  if (status.getState() == "SUCCEEDED") {     // branch on the result
    publish(input);
  } else {
    flagForReview(input);
  }
}

Independent work runs concurrently with ParallelExecution.fork(…) plus allOf(…) (a FORK and JOIN), and any other @WorkflowMethod can be called as a sub-workflow just by listing it in workflowNames:

@WorkflowStub(
    taskNames = {"movieapp.getMovie", "movieapp.enrichMovie", "movieapp.getArtwork",
                 "movieapp.refreshCache", "movieapp.publishPage"},
    workflowNames = {"movieapp.localize_page_workflow"})
public interface MoviePageWorkflows {
  // stubs not shown for brevity
  @WorkflowMethod(name = "prepare_movie_page", ownerEmail = "team@netflix.com")
  default void prepareMoviePage(MoviePageInput input) {
    // three independent branches, run in parallel
    Fork<WrappedMovie> details = ParallelExecution.fork(() -> {
      Movie movie = getMovie(input.getMovieId());
      return enrichMovie(movie);
    });
    Fork<Artwork> art = ParallelExecution.fork(() -> getArtwork(input.getMovieId()));
    Fork<Void> cache = ParallelExecution.fork(this::refreshCache);

    ParallelExecution.allOf(details, art, cache);   // FORK_JOIN and JOIN

    WrappedMovie enriched = details.get();
    Artwork artwork = art.get();
    LocalizedPage localized = localizePageWorkflow(input);  // sub-workflow call

    publishPage(enriched, artwork, localized);
  }
}

Sharing tasks and workflows across applications

Teams shouldn’t re-implement common tasks. Listing another team’s task or workflow in your @WorkflowStub is enough to call it like a local method, or invoke it as a sub-workflow, and the shared POJO types (a Movie, say) come along directly, with no copy-pasting between codebases.

Feature parity and rapid adoption

The SDK is gaining rapid adoption and has become the primary choice for authoring new workflows at Netflix. We continue to invest in the developer experience, with intelligent IDE plugins, better debugging, and an integrated testing framework so that testing a workflow in code feels like testing any other code.

In production: Netflix Ads

Netflix Ads runs complex, multi-step processes on Conductor with the Workflow SDK, and three examples show the range. Creative ingestion is a heavily branching pipeline where the SDK turned a sprawling JSON blob into type-safe, testable code, and a sequential run strategy eliminated a duplicate-processing race by serializing work per creative. Advertiser certificate management automates a previously manual, hard-to-scale process across several system integrations, with downstream automation when certificates expire. And Data Clean Rooms are privacy-preserving environments where Netflix and a partner run joint analysis on shared data, built on the SDK from day one. Provisioning a clean room is a multi-day sequence (create at a vendor, wait for the partner to join, activate, and eventually archive) that previously relied on hand-rolled async polling. Re-authored as Conductor workflows, each phase became a durable, observable state machine with automatic retries, state that survives restarts, and long partner waits that yield rather than hold a thread.

The common thread is that the SDK made multi-process, multi-integration workflows easy to author and maintain, and let teams lean on Conductor’s reliability and visibility instead of hand-rolling retries and distributed locking.

What’s next

Like the last time we wrote about Conductor, the road ahead is less a fixed roadmap than a wish-list, a sense of where we’re headed, shaped by what teams keep asking for.

On scale, the demands keep growing. As Netflix expands into new content types, like live, games, and podcasts, we anticipate our workflow load could grow 5x in the coming year, and the engine work described above is what gives us confidence we can absorb it without re-architecting again.

On developer experience, the Workflow SDK now covers all task types, so the focus shifts to the experience around writing workflows: a richer integrated testing story so a workflow can be validated against real worker behavior as easily as any other code, deeper agent tooling such as skills, plugins, and MCPs, and safe schema evolution: a schema registry for shared tasks and workflows, with guardrails that block non-backward-compatible changes so they can evolve without breaking the teams that depend on it.

On execution control, sequential is only the first run strategy. A family of richer policies is on the roadmap, including running N at a time per key, idempotent de-duplication, keep-first and keep-latest, and combinations of these, to cover the coordination patterns teams currently hand-build. And managed tasks will keep expanding the ways Conductor can run compute directly, beyond today’s container and serverless function integrations.

None of this is exhaustive, and priorities shift with the workloads we take on. But the direction is consistent: keep the overhead low, keep authoring safe and simple, and keep widening the range of work a single workflow can reliably coordinate.

title: Running Apache Spark experiments in my sleep (and on a plane)
summary:
By Prashanth Gedde Narayanaswamy

As one of Netflix’s largest and critical data pipelines, member-sessionizer consolidates tens of billions of hourly client events, encompassing user taps, playbacks, and engagement signals, into individual viewing sessions per profile.

A quick two-week tuning effort spiraled into two months when standard approaches hit a wall. Because the failures only happened at full production scale, each test took hours, limiting me to just three or four attempts daily. The turning point was changing the goal: instead of trying to speed up a single run, I built a way to run and monitor multiple tests at once and track every result.

That mindset led to an unconventional setup: kicking off five Spark jobs at once and monitoring them over spotty inflight Wi-Fi during a day-long trip home, while cloud servers handled the actual heavy lifting. This post covers how I set up that loop, along with the Spark bottlenecks and memory quirks I uncovered along the way.

The Scale Dilemma: Small Samples Don’t Catch Scale Bugs

Standard engineering wisdom says that you should isolate bugs on small datasets to iterate quickly. That works for standard software bugs, but it fails completely for big data performance bottlenecks.

While upgrading our sessionization pipeline from a legacy logging architecture to a modern platform, the new job hit critical failures, including executor Out-Of-Memory (OOM) errors, severe shuffle spillage, and thousands of stage retries. None of these issues could be reproduced using sampled data. The failures only triggered at full production scale because of data skew: an idle Netflix tab left streaming overnight generates tens of thousands of telemetry events, while a typical session only produces a handful. A standard 1% sample misses these extreme long-tail sessions entirely.

To catch the real bugs, every test run had to execute against a full hour of unsampled production data, along with all the deployment overhead that came with it.

The Strategy: Branch-Driven Isolation

The biggest win came from a feature in Dataflow, Netflix’s command-line tool for building, testing, and deploying data pipelines. It supports branch-driven development: our workflows run on Maestro (Netflix’s workflow orchestrator), which schedules and executes the jobs, and they already use a sanitized branch name (the ${dataflow.sanitizedbranch} placeholder). So if I push a branch like pgn/cap-experiment, then the deployed workflow, its tables, and its run namespace all get tagged with that branch name. This eliminates collisions with team members or between my own concurrent runs.

With that isolation in place, the model was simple: one branch is one independent experiment. I parameterized the scheduler (cap size, shuffle partitions, heavy-device threshold, feature flags) and gave each variant its own branch and output table. Instead of queuing five sequential tests over 10 hours, I fired off five variants simultaneously against the same time window. Total execution time dropped from the sum of all runs to just the length of the single slowest job.

Managing per-branch tables added zero overhead. Dataflow provisions and updates tables automatically from declared schemas without manual DDL. Whenever I modified the event bag structure between experiments, the table schema updated seamlessly, no CREATE TABLE or ALTER TABLE required.

The only real constraint was cluster contention. Because these heavy Spark jobs shared resources with the rest of the company, peak hours sometimes limited me to two concurrent runs instead of five. But even running two or three jobs in parallel was a massive improvement over single-threaded debugging.

The key takeaway: don’t focus on making a single multi-hour run faster, build a setup where you can run many experiments simultaneously without them stepping on each other.

While the previous chart shows the time savings, the architecture that enables this isolation looks like below:

How an AI Agent Helped

Running five parallel experiments gets messy fast. Tracking instance IDs, configs, memory spills, and stage failures across variants makes it easy to lose track.

This is where an AI agent stepped in, not to write clever code, but to handle operational grunt work. I described variants in plain English, and the agent updated scheduler configs, deployed to the branch, triggered jobs, and polled metrics. Once complete, it compared spill and failure counts across variants in a summary table, allowing me to ask, “Which run is closest to OOM-free at peak load?” and get an immediate answer.

The value wasn’t deep Spark expertise, but operational memory. It turned tedious Spark UI cross-checks into a single prompt.

Eventually, I packaged this workflow into a reusable agent skill (.agents/skills/sandbox-deploy-and-run/) run via /sandbox-deploy-and-run <module> <scheduler-file> [PARAM=value]. It handles the full lifecycle—preflight, deploy, background polling, auto-diagnostics, and re-entrant resume <instance_id> support—turning multi-hour experiments into a single command.

Why tmux Mattered

All of this ran on Workbench, Netflix’s cloud dev environment, using my laptop as a thin terminal. Without session persistence, an SSH drop or sleeping laptop would kill multi-hour Spark runs mid-flight.

tmux running directly on Workbench solved this. Every experiment lived in a named cloud session: I could close my laptop, reattach hours later, and pick up where I left off. Combined with branch isolation, this made "start five and walk away" possible.

This is now my default setup: a local terminal (Ghostty), dedicated git worktrees per branch, and persistent tmux sessions on Workbench. The local laptop is disposable—closing it or losing network never interrupts the jobs.

That setup turned a long travel day into active iteration time. I kicked off batches at the gate, checked results via AI agent over spotty inflight Wi-Fi, and squeezed 4–5 full experiment cycles into a single 24-hour flight.

What All Experiments Uncovered

The root cause came down to a single operator: collect_list. Because Spark buffers each full event bag in memory, long-session OOMs were driven by individual bag size, not total dataset volume. The legacy pipeline handled identical row counts without crashing, proving that each event in the new bag had grown significantly heavier.

Two factors inflated event weight:

  • Field types and Option boxing: The session ID changed from an 8-byte Long to a UUID string. Worse, wrapping fields in Scala Option forced Spark to deserialize typed Datasets into JVM objects (Some wrappers), driving up object allocation and GC pressure across tens of thousands of events per session.
  • Bloated string attributes: Low-value fields (e.g., referrer URLs, test allocations) added several hundred bytes per event. Multiplying these strings across collect_list wasted terabytes per hour, even though downstream tasks rarely used them.

The Fixes:

  1. Unboxed primitives: Removing Option wrappers from non-nullable fields dropped peak executor memory from 112% to 58% of the slot with zero disk spill.
  2. Slimmed event bags: Dropped unused per-event attributes and hoisted session-invariant metadata (app version, country) up to the session header.

Takeaway: Reducing individual event weight delivered far better stability than throwing more cluster memory at the problem.

Two Experiments That Changed My Mind

Out of dozens of runs, two findings completely overturned my assumptions about Spark memory management:

  • Finding 1: Narrowing rows can trigger faster OOMs. Slimming our table dropped its size below Spark’s auto-broadcast threshold, prompting the query planner to switch from shuffle joins to broadcast joins. Because broadcast joins pin build-side tables directly into executor memory, narrower rows actually increased total memory pressure.
  • Finding 2: Broadcast hash joins were silently draining memory. Adaptive Query Execution (AQE) rewrote nine sort-merge joins into broadcast hash joins at runtime. While each join stayed under our 400 MB broadcast limit individually, AQE pinned ~3.1 GB of cumulative data simultaneously in a single executor, pushing containers over the edge.

The Surgical Fix: Instead of disabling broadcast joins globally, I lowered only AQE’s runtime threshold (spark.sql.adaptive.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold) to 10 MB while leaving the compile-time threshold untouched. That single change freed up ~3.1 GB of executor memory without impacting initial query planning.

Takeaway: Broadcast joins speed up queries, but pinned memory isn’t free. Watch accumulated broadcasts in your execution plan, not just dataset sizes.

Keeping a Single Experiment Log

When running dozens of parallel tests, the biggest risk isn’t job failure, it’s losing track of what you’ve already tried or confusing which JAR and config produced a result.

To solve this, I scaffolded the AI agent to append a row to a repository Markdown table after every run:

  • Run # | Jar ver | Change vs. Previous Run | Config | Key Metrics (Spill, Failed Tasks, Peak Memory, Duration)

If a run yielded a key finding, the agent added a short note explaining what the result proved or disproved.

Key Takeaways:

  • Single source of truth: It created an auditable history for the entire investigation.
  • Forced discipline: Requiring “Change vs. Previous Run” forced me to isolate variables. Whenever I bundled multiple changes, I couldn’t isolate the root cause and had to rerun the test — a mistake the log format immediately exposed.

A secondary doc (events-join-spark-tuning.md) captured the distilled findings as a quick "symptom-to-knob" lookup, so teammates didn't have to wade through the full chronological history.

A Mistake I Learned From: The Fix That Only Worked Off-Peak.

To cap session size, I added row_number().over(Window...) and filtered for the first N events. It passed off-peak tests cleanly, but crashed with OOMs at peak load.

The issue was structural: Spark’s Window operator buffers an entire session in memory before evaluating row numbers and filtering. The cap trimmed output downstream, but it didn't limit memory usage during buffering, so a single skewed session overwhelmed executor memory.

The Fix & Lesson: We moved truncation ahead of the Window stage to cap events before buffering occurs.

Takeaway: Test fixes against worst-case input skew. Off-peak runs hide structural bottlenecks that peak scale will immediately trigger.

The final fix

Pulling it together, four changes shipped, each isolated to a single experiment before it landed:

  • Unboxed the never-null fields from Option to plain primitives. Peak executor memory dropped from about 112% of the slot to about 58%, with zero spill.
  • Slimmed the event bag. Dropped per-event fields nobody used, and hoisted session-invariant fields (versions, country, connection type) to the session level so they are stored once per session, not once per event.
  • Capped session size before the Window stage. Dropped oversized sessions ahead of the buffering, and truncated the bag to the cap rather than dropping whole sessions.
  • Lowered AQE’s runtime broadcast threshold. Set spark.sql.adaptive.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold to 10 MB, leaving the compile-time threshold untouched.

The Unresolved Bottleneck

While these fixes made the pipeline run cleanly, they didn’t solve the underlying scaling issue: aggregating an entire session’s event bag into a single row has a hard ceiling. As our upstream telemetry source evolves and adds new attributes, each event in the bag becomes heavier, meaning this memory pressure will eventually return without a single line of code changing on our end.

Slimming and unboxing bought us headroom, but they didn’t change the fundamental data shape. The biggest takeaway from this effort is that tuning buys time, not infinite scale. If your underlying data model allows unbounded row growth, tuning alone won’t save you , eventually, the architecture itself has to change.

Summary

  • If the bug only appears at scale, stop trying to sample. Build a way to run many full-scale runs in parallel instead.
  • If your scheduler can use the branch name, then one branch becomes one isolated experiment, and running many at once becomes easy.
  • Use an AI agent to run the operation, not only to write code. Deploy, poll, pull metrics, compare variants: this is where most of the time goes.
  • Once a loop repeats, package it as a skill. The deploy-run-watch-diagnose cycle becomes one command.
  • Use tmux for long runs. The run must survive you closing the laptop.
  • Keep one single experiment log, and make every entry state the one change from the previous run. The format itself forces you to change one variable at a time.
  • For memory problems, look at the per-row width first, not only at the total data volume. Bigger field types, Option boxing, and fat unused strings all add up inside a collect_list bag.
  • Tuning buys headroom, not a new ceiling. If the data shape can grow without a bound, the design has to change eventually, tuning alone will not save you.

title: Netflix Stratum Media Processing: Automated Container Right-Sizing
summary:
By Violetta Pidvolotska and Naveen Mareddy

Stratum is Netflix’s internal serverless media processing platform, shaped by over a decade of experience developing large-scale distributed systems. It powers a wide range of media workloads — including encoding, packaging, inspection, and quality scoring — behind playback, advertising, studio workflows, AI embeddings, and more.

Engineers develop Stratum functions by packaging application code and OS dependencies into OCI images. Stratum then schedules these containers as batch jobs on Netflix’s Titus compute platform, with upstream services triggering function executions.

Every day, Stratum manages hundreds of thousands of containers across bursty, high-throughput, and latency-sensitive workloads. As Netflix’s core media processing platform, this load needs to scale as new content formats enter the catalog, such as podcasts, live events, sports, ads, or regional ingests like TF1 in France.

To request resources for these functions, owners specify their CPU, memory, disk, and network limits as YAML configuration, as shown below:

functionName: VideoEncoder.encodeV1
resources:
  numCpus: 8
  memoryInMB: 18000
  diskSizeInMB: 50000
  networkInMbps: 1000

Maintaining optimal values manually is challenging amidst evolving Netflix infrastructure, EC2 instance upgrades, and application-level changes. Consequently, configs are often over-provisioned upfront or slowly drift away from their ideal values over time. Mis-sized configurations are a universal pain of large-scale serverless platforms, causing additional cognitive load for function builders and operational costs for platform owners.

In this post, we share how we built the Stratum Resource Tuner (SRT) — an automated system that safely right-sizes running containers in production without human intervention. We will walk through real-world examples, our safety architecture, and what we learned when an automated change went wrong.

The Challenge: Over-Provisioning

When engineers write a new Stratum function, they typically copy a resource YAML from an existing function or size it for the absolute worst-case scenario. Once running in production, engineers rarely revisit these configurations until a failure occurs, prompting them to over-provision resources out of an abundance of caution.

Manual resource tuning does not scale for the following reasons:

  • High Operational Friction: Downsizing requires days of manual metric monitoring and trial-and-error testing, diverting valuable engineering cycles away from other high-impact work. If a cut goes too far, engineers face production incidents — making manual tuning a high-risk, low-reward task.
  • Continuous Infrastructure & Codec Evolution: Cloud providers regularly upgrade their hardware. A resource allocation that was optimal on an older hardware generation quietly becomes inefficient on newer hardware. At the same time, Netflix continuously advances media standards and improves encoding algorithms (such as AV1, AV2, and spatial audio). An allocation tuned for one codec might not be optimal when an improved algorithm is released.
  • Dynamic Workload Evolution: As Netflix expands into new media types — such as streaming video podcasts, sports, interactive AI-adapted ad formats, and major broadcaster integrations like TF1 in France — media processing footprints can change unpredictably, rendering static container resource limits imprecise.
  • Rising Industry Hardware Costs: Driven by massive global AI infrastructure demand, server hardware and DRAM prices continue to climb, making idle container memory significantly more expensive to waste.
  • Compounding Platform Scale: At Netflix scale, even minor over-provisioning multiplies exponentially across hundreds of thousands of daily container executions, compounding wasted capacity across the entire Stratum platform.

To understand the scale of the challenge, we analyzed historical usage across Stratum’s workloads. The telemetry confirmed our hypothesis: over-provisioning was frequent, wasted compute was compounding, and the sustainable path forward required a fundamental re-evaluation of how resource configurations are managed.

Meet the Stratum Resource Tuner

To address the challenges listed above, we built the Stratum Resource Tuner (SRT) to automatically right-size Stratum containers. Our north star is to ensure that users never have to manually specify the resource configurations. We started with a handful of high-throughput workloads with relaxed latency requirements, which account for the majority (70%–80%) of resource usage.

As a quick note on terminology, we use “right-sizing” and “tuning” interchangeably in this post. “Downsizing” means decreasing resource limits, while “upsizing” means increasing them. Since our goal is to optimize for cost, this post focuses on downsizing.

Automatic right-sizing is not enabled by default. Function owners must manually opt in on a per resource type basis (e.g., CPU, memory, network, or disk). Once enrolled, SRT operates without a human in the loop across five steps:

  1. Collect resource usage metrics across all executions of that function.
  2. Generate a recommendation for each resource type (e.g., CPU or memory).
  3. Verify the recommendation through experiments.
  4. Apply or reject the recommendation based on the results of experiments.
  5. Monitor post-apply metrics, watching for anomalies after applying the recommendation.

“Recommendation” is a key construct in SRT and serves as the primary unit of operation. As SRT executes its steps, it promotes the recommendation through several stages:

  • CREATED: A scheduled workflow generated the recommendation.
  • EVALUATING: Recommendation verification is running, and SRT is analyzing the results.
  • APPLIED: All experiments passed, and SRT automatically rolled out the recommended configuration.
  • REJECTED: At least one experiment failed, leaving the function configuration untouched.
  • MONITORED: SRT monitors the recommendation during a post-apply soak period to verify stability.

The sections below examine each of these stages in detail. To illustrate the flow, we will follow the real-world lifecycle of the VideoEncoder.encodeV1 function — a high-throughput video encoding function whose over-provisioned memory and CPU footprints were successfully tuned.

Note that all operational thresholds and safety limits discussed below are fully configurable per function to accommodate varying workload characteristics and risk tolerances.

Metrics Collection

To make these recommendations possible, we need a solid metrics collection mechanism. Every Stratum container reports its function execution metadata, infrastructure dimensions, and resource utilization (CPU, memory, disk, and network) at sub-minute resolution.

These metrics flow through Keystone, Netflix’s real-time event streaming platform, and land in two separate datastores:

  • Execution summaries store: Stores execution-level summary metrics indexed in Elasticsearch for fast point lookups, serving as our short-term datastore for querying and inspecting individual runs.
  • High-resolution long-term store: Stores raw, high-resolution usage metrics in Iceberg tables. While slower to query, it serves as our long-term datastore, holding months of history for resource utilization trend analysis.

One record is written per execution, which is represented as a span. Here is how these records look for a single span of our VideoEncoder.encodeV1 function.

In Elasticsearch, the record captures the high-level summary of the completed span, identified by tags.stratum.spanId:

  "tags.stratum.spanId": "38536313f65f060a",
  "tags.functionName": "VideoEncoder.encodeV1",

   { "cpu_usage": 2.25, "memory_mb": 3584.09, "disk_mb": 25410.1, "net_in_mb": 0.02, "net_out_mb": 0.05 },
   { "cpu_usage": 4.16, "memory_mb": 6750.79, "disk_mb": 30400.5, "net_in_mb": 165.90, "net_out_mb": 0.38 },
   ... 
  ]
}

Recommendation Generation

A scheduled Conductor workflow runs daily, reading the past month of usage data from Iceberg and generating recommendations for every function and resource type. The workflow also generates recommendations for functions that have not opted into automatic right-sizing to preview potential savings.

Each recommendation is saved in the recommendations datastore, enabling us to query and filter recommendations by function, resource type, or status on an ad hoc basis.

For each function and resource type, the workflow applies the following generation logic:

  • Filter by workload type: We only tune high-throughput workloads. This focuses our efforts on right-sizing, which yields the most meaningful fleet-wide savings.
  • Aggressively tune CPU and network: We target p99 usage with no extra headroom. CPU and network are compressible resources; if a container occasionally hits these limits, the function might execute slightly slower.
  • Conservatively tune memory and disk: We target p99.9 usage and include a safety buffer. Running out of physical memory or disk space causes hard failures — such as Out of Memory (OOM) or Out of Disk (OOD) crashes — making a protective margin essential.
  • Apply safeguards to changes: We discard recommendations if the absolute reduction is too small to justify operational effort. For memory and disk, we clamp the maximum reduction allowed in a single cycle to 15% — a safety limit introduced after learning from early production runs.

The workflow creates new recommendations in the CREATED state. If a recommendation already exists in this state for a given function and resource type, SRT overwrites it with updated calculations. Once a recommendation advances past the CREATED state, its recommended_value and stats fields become immutable. Subsequent daily runs generate a new recommendation with a unique ID instead of modifying the existing record.

As the recommendation moves through its lifecycle, SRT populates the remaining parameters.

When proceeding to the verification stage, SRT transitions the recommendation status to EVALUATING, records the target experiment settings, and links the active workflow execution tracking the experiment.

Finally, once verification runs complete, the status changes to APPLIED or REJECTED, storing the outcome details and completion timestamp for analysis.

Retry with More Resources

We take a conservative approach to generating recommendations, prioritizing system stability over extreme efficiency. Because recommendations rely on historical usage data, they cannot always anticipate sudden spikes or novel workload profiles when functions encounter heavy, unseen requests.

To handle these unexpected spikes, we developed a fail-safe mechanism. A watcher process running in each tuned container tracks memory and disk usage during function execution. If the container exceeds the pre-set thresholds, 85% for non-cached memory usage or 95% for disk usage, the watcher flags the execution as high risk, cancels execution, and re-queues the task onto a larger container:

new_container_size = original_container_size * 1.5

This 1.5 multiplier only applies to memory and disk dimensions.

This “retry with more resources” mechanism serves as our safety net: larger container configurations are applied only when retrying tasks to self-heal from edge cases. Although these infrequent retries incur additional compute costs and latency, they allow us to keep day-to-day configurations highly optimized without having to size for rare, costly outliers up front.

For our VideoEncoder.encodeV1 function, if a heavy run causes memory usage to exceed the 85% threshold (15,300 MB) within its current 18,000 MB container, the system aborts the execution and reruns it on a 27,000 MB container.

While we prefer to trigger retries based on actual OOM or OOD events rather than pre-set thresholds, technical constraints in our current architecture make true event detection challenging. Using pre-set thresholds serves as a reliable stopgap while we develop improved detection capabilities.

SRT automatically enables the retry mechanism for any function opted into memory or disk right-sizing. Each Stratum container reports retry events, which flow into Elasticsearch and Iceberg alongside standard performance telemetry.

Recommendation Verification

Every recommendation must pass a two-stage verification process managed by a Conductor workflow before rollout. During this EVALUATING stage, SRT executes two distinct experiment types:

  1. Synthetic experiment: A low-cost, low-risk test to catch obvious regressions before production rollout.
  2. Production experiment: A live evaluation that validates changes across diverse production workloads to increase confidence.

A recommendation advances to production testing only after passing the synthetic experiment. When an opted-in function has multiple pending recommendations, SRT prioritizes and evaluates the candidates with the highest estimated savings first.

Synthetic experiment:

  • Runs in a test environment isolated from production traffic.
  • Sets up two clusters: one for the current and one for the recommended config.
  • Replays identical request sets across both clusters simultaneously without splitting traffic, exposing both configurations to 100% of test requests.
  • Typically runs for 1–2 hours.
  • Runs to completion without early termination checks.

Production experiment:

  • Runs in production on real user traffic, split three ways:
    ◦ ~90% remains on the main cluster (current production config).
    ◦ ~5% goes to a baseline cluster (current production config).
    ◦ ~5% goes to an experimental cluster (recommendation config).
  • Evaluates recommendations against a similarly sized baseline cluster rather than the main cluster to preserve comparable traffic profiles.
  • Typically runs from one day to one week, depending on traffic volume.
  • Fails fast: cancels the experiment early if regressions are detected.

The Stratum platform executes other experiments alongside SRT experiments. To avoid over-splitting traffic, SRT experiments run at lower priority and yield resources to active, higher-priority experiments.

Traffic arrives in irregular bursts separated by multi-day or multi-week lulls. The verification pipeline accommodates these variable arrival patterns rather than expecting steady traffic.

Back to our VideoEncoder.encodeV1 memory recommendation (18,000 MB → 15,300 MB), verification is triggered with:

{
  "recommendationId": "2edb734a-6184-4f5e-8ffa-23004bd665d7",
  "syntheticExperiment": { "numberOfExecutions": 3000 },
  "productionExperiment": {
    "enabled": true,
    "maxContainers": 20, // max containers shift to baseline & experimental clusters
    "upGateTimeoutMinutes": 10080, // time to wait for traffic to start flowing
    "maxRunDurationMinutes": 1240, // max time to run the experiment once traffic starts
    "minSamples": 500 // min executions needed on both clusters before evaluating
  }
}

Both verification stages evaluate recommendations against two sequential checks, terminating immediately if either fails:

  • Retries with more resources: Restricts memory and disk downsizes to a maximum 1% retry threshold over the experiment duration.
  • Execution time: Compares median runtimes to prevent outlier distortion, permitting up to a 10–15% slowdown relative to baseline, depending on workload, and is configurable by function.

If a recommendation passes both verification stages, SRT updates its status to APPLIED and rolls out the configuration to the main production cluster. If a check fails at any point, SRT marks the recommendation as REJECTED and preserves the existing configuration. SRT sends notifications for both outcomes.

For VideoEncoder.encodeV1, both stages passed cleanly:

  "outcome": "APPLIED",
  "syntheticExperiment": {
    "result": "SUCCESS",
    "samples": { "baseline": 3000, "experimental": 3000 },
    "medianExecutionSecs": { "baseline": 59.0, "experimental": 59.0 },
    "slownessIncreasePct": 0.0,
    "retryRatePct": { "baseline": 0.0, "experimental": 0.0 }
  },
  "productionExperiment": {
    "result": "SUCCESS",
    "samples": { "baseline": 50361, "experimental": 49790 },
    "medianExecutionSecs": { "baseline": 196.0, "experimental": 198.0 },
    "slownessIncreasePct": 1.0,
    "retryRatePct": { "baseline": 0.0, "experimental": 0.0 }
  }
}

The recommendation moved to the APPLIED state, permanently setting the memory allocation for VideoEncoder.encodeV1 to 15,300 MB. We observed similarly clean results for the CPU recommendation, which reduced CPU allocation from 8 cores to 4.

Post-Apply Monitoring

Passing verification experiments does not mark the end of the recommendation lifecycle. Updated function code, modified input parameters, or underlying changes in the compute environment (Titus/EC2) can alter production behavior over time. To ensure configuration safety and foster feature adoption, we instituted continuous post-apply monitoring for applied changes.

We monitor metrics for 90 days across two rolling time windows: a 30-minute fast window and a 24-hour slow window. Each window maintains specific alert thresholds: a 3% retry rate over 30 minutes or a 2% rate over 24 hours triggers an automated notification.

At steady state, workloads exhibit baseline retry rates around 0.1%, with rates up to 2%–3% falling within acceptable operational variances. Most applied recommendations remained stable over the past three months.

VideoEncoder.encodeV1 has operated on its tuned configuration for months without breaching thresholds. However, VideoEncoder.encodeV2 presented a challenging edge case: a 50% memory reduction passed all verification checks and ran stably for two weeks before an unexpected traffic shift drove retry rates above 60%.

Because early versions lacked automated rollback capabilities, engineers manually triaged exception cases. This incident highlighted the need for automated mitigation, prompting us to construct self-healing rollback functionality.

Today, the two auto-revert windows look like this:

  • Last 30 minutes: 3% retries warn us; 10% triggers an auto-revert.
  • Last 24 hours: A 2% retry rate triggers both an alert and an automatic revert.

Breaching an auto-revert threshold immediately restores the function configuration to its pre-recommendation baseline.

We intentionally maintain straightforward revert logic — restoring the last known stable configuration rather than attempting dynamic resource adjustments during an incident.

The VideoEncoder.encodeV2 incident also reshaped our recommendation generation rules for memory and disk allocations. Rather than applying full target reductions immediately, SRT now applies smaller, incremental 15% step changes, advancing only after confirming stability at each step. Additionally, we introduced a global kill switch to disable automated right-sizing across all functions in case of unexpected issues or side effects.

Additionally, we enforce a mandatory cooldown period — typically one week — before initiating new experiments on a function. Pausing adjustments allows us to observe performance across diverse production traffic patterns, identifying potential risks before applying subsequent recommendations.

Where Are We Today

Oversized containers and config drift don’t have to be an accepted tax of running serverless workloads at scale. By building the Stratum Resource Tuner, we transformed manual, risk-averse resource sizing into an automated, self-healing pipeline. Through real-world workloads and hard lessons from unexpected spikes, we’ve proven that continuous right-sizing can safely deliver significant gains in infrastructure efficiency.

We initially focused on right-sizing high-throughput video encoding workloads, aiming for an initial 5% reduction in overall Stratum compute costs. For instance, VideoEncoder.encodeV1 achieved a 50% reduction in CPU usage and 40% in memory usage without compromising performance or retry rates.

However, edge cases like VideoEncoder.encodeV2 highlighted key lessons: large single-step reductions can introduce hidden risks, and manual incident response slows recovery. These insights led us to enforce stricter safety guardrails in the Stratum Resource Tuner, including capping memory and disk reductions at 15% per cycle and adding automated rollbacks when retry thresholds are breached. Guided by these safeguards, re-tuning VideoEncoder.encodeV2 yielded a stable 20% memory reduction with zero subsequent incidents.

Looking ahead, our key priorities include:

  • Expand SRT beyond high-throughput encoding workloads to support a wider variety of functions and workload types.
  • Further tune the resources in regions with constrained resource availability.
  • Move from reactive alerts to proactive, automated upsizing for under-provisioned functions.
  • Experiment with intentional upsizing for latency-sensitive workloads to evaluate performance gains and reduce function execution time.
  • Upgrade our failure signals for OOM/OOD events from lagging indicators to leading indicators to improve tuning precision.
